name: SLC35A2-CDG (UDP-galactose transporter)
aliases: congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIm

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: An X-linked CDG caused by defective transport of UDP-galactose into the Golgi, impairing galactosylation of N-glycans
Presents chiefly as an early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, frequently with infantile spasms and hypsarrhythmia, with developmental delay and hypotonia
Because it is X-linked with somatic mosaicism, phenotypic severity varies and the transferrin pattern can normalise with age, so a normal screen does not exclude it
Transferrin analysis, when abnormal, shows a type II pattern reflecting loss of terminal galactose from glycan antennae
It is one of the potentially treatable CDG subtypes, in which oral galactose supplementation may improve glycosylation and, in some patients, seizures and biochemical markers
Coagulation, endocrine and dysmorphic features are generally milder than in classic PMM2-CDG
Diagnosis rests on SLC35A2 sequencing, increasingly identified through epilepsy gene panels and exome sequencing
reference.pathophysiology: SLC35A2 encodes the Golgi UDP-galactose transporter that supplies the nucleotide sugar donor for galactosyltransferases. Impaired transport starves the Golgi of UDP-galactose, so galactose is not added to maturing complex N-glycans, leaving truncated antennae and defining a type II processing defect on transferrin analysis. Because the gene is X-linked and the disorder often arises from somatic mosaic variants, the degree of hypoglycosylation and its clinical impact are variable. Providing galactose can partially bypass the transport bottleneck, which underlies the observed biochemical and sometimes clinical response.
additionalDifferentials: Other early-onset epileptic encephalopathies (e.g. genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathies)
Other type II CDG subtypes such as TMEM165-CDG and B4GALT1-CDG
PMM2-CDG and other type I disorders when the transferrin pattern is intermediate
Structural or metabolic causes of infantile spasms
Glucose transporter and other treatable metabolic epilepsies
additionalInvestigations: Transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry (may be normal, so does not exclude the diagnosis)
SLC35A2 molecular genetic testing, including assessment for somatic mosaicism
Electroencephalography for hypsarrhythmia or other epileptic patterns
Neuroimaging for structural or malformative changes
Trial of galactose supplementation with biochemical monitoring in confirmed cases
redFlags: Infantile spasms or drug-resistant seizures requiring prompt evaluation
Failure to thrive with feeding difficulty
A normal transferrin screen in a child with a compatible phenotype, which should not stop genetic testing
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable and generally dominated by the severity of the epilepsy and developmental delay; some patients show biochemical and clinical improvement with galactose, though epilepsy can remain difficult to control. Milder mosaic presentations exist.
pitfalls: Excluding SLC35A2-CDG on the basis of a normal transferrin test
Missing somatic mosaicism if only standard blood testing is performed
Failing to consider a galactose trial in confirmed cases
Attributing the epilepsy solely to a primary channelopathy without metabolic evaluation
references: Scriver's OMMBID, congenital disorders of glycosylation
Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics, disorders of glycosylation
management: Give oral galactose supplementation to partially bypass the transport defect and improve N-glycan galactosylation, with biochemical monitoring
Control the epileptic encephalopathy with antiseizure medication and standard treatment of infantile spasms using hormonal therapy or vigabatrin
Provide developmental support with physiotherapy and occupational and speech therapy for delay and hypotonia
Monitor transferrin glycoforms and clinical response to galactose, recognising that the transferrin pattern may normalise with age
Offer genetic counselling addressing X-linked inheritance and somatic mosaicism
Coordinate multidisciplinary metabolic, neurology and neurodevelopmental follow-up
